items.title: Listen: The imperfect world of pulsars
items.summary: Here in the Universe, there are a few things that are as close-to-perfect as can be. The Sun, for instance is the roundest object in the Universe, but other stars are rounder, with white dwarfs and neutron stars exhibiting even more perfectly roundness. Meanwhile, in terms of keeping time, we might think of the spinning Earth as a wonderful clock — after all, we base our calendar off of it — but the Earth spins down over time and changes its distance from the Sun: both factors that lead to it being rather imperfect as a timekeeper, especially over the long run. For keeping time, it turns out that the best natural clocks in the Universe are millisecond pulsars . It’s possible to look at a millisecond pulsar, measure its timing, and then look away for extremely long periods of time, like perhaps a year, and then when you return to it, know whether a billion pulses have elapsed or a billion-and-one pulses have elapsed. It’s fascinating how these objects come to be, as well as how regularly they pulse, but recently an unexpected instability has been discovered within them: pulse profile changes, where the amount of energy and when its released during each pulse can change from one interval to the next. The co-discoverer of pulse profile changes in millisecond pulsar J0437-4715 , PhD candidate Rami Mandow of Macquarie University joins us as our guest for this all-new edition of the Starts With A Bang podcast . If you’ve ever wondered what millisecond pulsars are, where they come from, how they evolve, and what makes them the best cosmic clocks of all, you’re not alone. But if you’ve ever wondered about just how imperfect and unstable they are, welcome to the frontiers of astrophysics, where we’re just discovering a slightly less-perfect Universe than we ever realized we were inhabiting before! items.title: Rebuilding a World That Never Existed
items.summary: This is an edition of the Books Briefing, our editors’ weekly guide to the best in books. Sign up for it here. When it comes to reading, I’m not a glutton for punishment—I didn’t get very far into Finnegans Wake —but I am drawn to interesting challenges. Among the most memorably difficult reads I’ve taken on was the 1926 book A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle . A cerebral but darkly funny epic poem whose plot is well summarized by its title, it is written in “synthetic Scots,” a language cobbled together from Scottish dialects by its author, Hugh MacDiarmid. (Although Scots survives as a minority language with many regional variations, none of them closely resemble MacDiarmid’s concoction.) I loved the verse for its woozy lyricism and nerded out on the text’s annotations; I was also fascinated by the author’s grand ambitions. MacDiarmid was part of a cultural movement known as the Scottish Renaissance, whose writers sought to revive the once-independent nation’s dialects and traditions. But did he really think he could kick off a national resurgence by inventing a language no reader could easily understand? And what would drive a writer to even try? This week, the Atlantic staff writer Lily Meyer explored a similar question in her article about What Remains , a novel written by Brais Lamela in Galician. First, here are six new stories from The Atlantic ’s Books section: The one source Bob Woodward can’t get to talk How to be an ethical Russophile The worst thing about AI writing “Memories of the Train,” a short story by Siqi Liu AI is destroying the trust between writers and readers. “Poem for the WaterShed,” a poem by Gretel Ehrlich Meyer calls Lamela’s choice to write in a language primarily spoken in a single region in the northwest of Spain “an artistic expression of commitment to his particular roots,” and it is—but Lamela also understands the futility of trying to re-create the past. The novel’s narrator is writing a thesis about a widow in Galicia, who resisted the dictator Francisco Franco’s effort to subjugate the area (the government flooded rural villages and banned the Galician language). Yet the narrator’s academic ambitions are as nostalgic as they are political. Feeling rootless and isolated in New York, he hopes, Meyer writes, “to create a home of some sort for the unsettled parts of himself.” Other authors in minority languages have been vocal about their motivations. Writers in Greenlandic, Basque, Welsh, and the Judeo-Spanish language of Ladino have eschewed dominant languages such as Spanish or English to preserve cultures that have been subsumed by larger nations. Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o forsook English to write in Kikuyu, publicly rebelling against England’s rule in Kenya and explaining that he wanted to “reconnect to the patriotic traditions” of a “literature rooted among the people.” MacDiarmid, too, saw himself as resisting the English and their language; he hated them so much that he once wrote, in private correspondence, that he might prefer a Nazi victory over England. But unlike Ngũgĩ, who wrote in a language spoken by millions, the Scot was trying to build a lexicon that had never really existed. In this sense he is not unlike Lamela’s narrator, a person who finds “re-creation” to be, Meyer writes, “a source of stability as much as it is an escape.” Characters like this, Meyer adds, “aspire to inhabit history so fully that they might create a home, or at least a moment of rest and acknowledgment, for its unsettled ghosts.” Such attempts might be doomed to fail, but that doesn’t mean they aren’t noble, or even beautiful. MacDiarmid didn’t exactly rebuild Scottish literature, but he made a modernist work of art that I’ll never forget. Illustration by Adam Maida / The Atlantic A Novel About Obsessively Digging Into the Past By Lily Meyer A new book by the Galician writer Brais Lamela chronicles the drive that many have to touch history, no matter how elusive it is. Read the full article. What to Read Dirtbag, Massachusetts , by Isaac Fitzgerald Though his memoir-in-essays is subtitled A Confessional , and though it opens by revising the story he and his family used to tell about his childhood, Fitzgerald doesn’t immediately lay bare the lingering pain of his tumultuous upbringing. The first 11 essays are plenty vulnerable: Fitzgerald writes that he was born of an affair; spent his early years living in a homeless shelter and then in low-income housing run by the Catholic Worker movement; moved to north-central Massachusetts, where “violence was the solution, problem, and consequence”; and began abusing alcohol and drugs before age 13. But these are mere “flashes of the past,” as Fitzgerald writes in the last essay, “My Story,” where he takes full control of the narrative of his life. As he admits to having avoided the full truth, Fitzgerald becomes his own confessor, the one with the power to forgive. — Kristen Martin From our list: Six books you should read twice Out Next Week 📚 On the Calculation of Volume (Book V) , by Solvej Balle 📚 The Imperfect City , by Paul Goldberger 📚 Love the Revolution , by Aleksandr I. Solzhenitsyn Your Weekend Read Illustration by Tina Zhou / The Atlantic Zelda ’s Midlife Crisis By Ian Bogost This idea, that a video game could facilitate exploration in a simulated world bigger than the challenges choreographed inside it, is now so familiar that it counts as cliché. But at the time, it was startling. Popular culture—even Star Wars —was not yet understood by its consumers as world building, a now-popular name for constructing a fictional universe and then situating characters and stories inside it. Tolkien had been popular for decades, of course, but high fantasy was still largely considered escapist and—apologies—somewhat cringeworthy. To obsess about a false world real enough to imagine occupying remained strange, a fixation of dweebs unable or unwilling to live in the real one. Read the full article. items.title: A modest proposal: Europe should go full bananas
items.summary: Underneath the political map of Europe’s nation-states simmers another reality: a tangle of economic and logistical corridors that transcend national borders. The best known of these is the Blue Banana. Many others aren’t as visible, and that is due to poor marketing: They lack an equally imaginative handle. Hence this modest proposal: If the European Union is serious about integration, it should get silly about names. All 12 of its major transnational economic corridors should be named after the bendy fruit. In other words, Europe should go full bananas. “Looks like a banana,” said the minister The Blue Banana — the first of the bunch, so to speak — is of surprisingly recent vintage. First proposed in 1989 by French geographer Roger Brunet as an economic zone with common characteristics, this urban-industrial belt runs from Manchester in northern England to Milan in northern Italy. A French minister remarked that Brunet’s area looked a bit like a banana, an illustrator for Le Nouvel Observateur colored it blue, and hey presto, the Blue Banana was born. That nickname did what mere economic stats can’t: It captured the imagination, thus highlighting a process that earlier maps had missed. In an increasingly borderless Europe, the logics of proximity and compatibility are creating zones of economic contiguity across multiple countries. Roger Brunet’s original map of what he called “the European backbone” (“la dorsale européenne”), later more memorably rebranded “the Blue Banana.” Credit : Roger Brunet, La France dans l’espace européen (1989), cited in Cahiers de santé publique It may lack a flag, an anthem, and a parliament, but the Blue Banana has a cartographic shape, an economic weight, and — thanks to a bendy fruit and a French magazine illustrator — a catchy name. Catchy names matter. They grab and focus attention — and attract investment. That is why some of Europe’s other international zones of economic similarity thought it useful to adopt the banana idea (see the Green, Yellow, Orange, and Golden Bananas). But many others haven’t, and Europe should do better than that half-hearted, haphazard approach. It’s sad to see economic corridors of consequence laboring under inauspicious names like STRING , which is something you lose in a drawer, or outright ominous ones like the Atlantic Axis, which sounds like a pact with a dictator that you probably shouldn’t have signed. An extra outlet for feelings of belonging Giving this whole group of regions a coordinated set of catchy names would not only increase their visibility but also help their inhabitants identify with them. Knowing which banana you are part of gives you an extra outlet for your feelings of belonging, one that transcends national borders. “Going bananas” may also help the EU refocus on achieving economic excellence rather than merely being a regulatory superpower, as it is today. Hence this map, showing all 12 major transnational economic corridors in Europe as their own bananas. There is strength in a union: You may crush a single banana, but you can’t bend a whole bunch! The Blue Banana is the big boy. Home to 110 million people, it is Western Europe’s industrial heartland, by some accounts generating up to 40% of the eurozone’s GDP. The Golden Banana (a.k.a. the Mediterranean Sunbelt or the “North of the South”) is the Blue Banana’s southern cousin. Curving from northwestern Italy through France’s Mediterranean coast into northeastern Spain, it combines high urban density with major ports and high levels of tourism. Following the coastline from Odesa, Ukraine, through Romania and Bulgaria to Istanbul, Turkey, the Orange Banana is the Black Sea’s answer to the Golden Banana. Its potential is considerable, lying as it does at the crossroads of the Black Sea, the Danube, and the Bosphorus. The Green Banana describes an urban-economic arc running from Gdańsk on the Baltic to Trieste on the Adriatic, bridging Poland, Czechia, Slovakia, Austria, Hungary, Slovenia, and Croatia. The potential for economic growth and integration in this area came into focus only after the collapse of communism in 1989. The last of the existing bananas is the Yellow Banana , running from Paris across Germany to Warsaw. Its east-west orientation is a deliberate counterweight to the Blue Banana, which runs north to south. Franco-German collaboration goes back to the founding of the European project in the 1950s. Adding Poland lends weight to that partnership and acknowledges the eastward expansion of the EU. Here is another, more fruitful way of looking at the map of Europe (pun fully intended): A Union of Bananas, transcending national borders, re-establishing old economic units and trade routes, and bringing together Europeans from different EU member states. Credit: Ruland Kolen/Claude The color of Hanseatic herring The other seven regions have rather unimaginative names — the comparison to a piece of tropical fruit would be an upgrade. Take STRING, which is bizarrely short for South Western Baltic Sea Trans-Regional Area — Implementing New Geography. It stretches from Hamburg via Copenhagen, Malmö, and Gothenburg to Oslo. Those cool cities would probably prefer a cool moniker like the Silver Banana , chosen for the color of the herring on which the Hanseatic League grew fat. As we mentioned, “axis” gives bad historical vibes. So, how about a Tawny Banana going from Spain’s A Coruña to Portugal’s Lisbon via Porto? The clue to the name is in the latter city and the tawny (i.e., yellowish-brown) port wine it produces, among several other varieties. Across the Gulf of Finland you could have the White Banana . The name recalls the white summer nights of the High North. However, the banana that unites the three major cities on the Gulf of Finland is incomplete: Helsinki and Tallinn may still be linked by intense flows of trade, traffic, tourism, and investment, but relations with Russia’s St. Petersburg are currently strained, to say the least. What other name could the economic corridor between Dublin in the Republic of Ireland and Belfast in Northern Ireland have but the Emerald Banana ? (Fortunately, Orange was already taken.) The Amber Banana follows the Rail Baltica corridor, from Tallinn via Riga and Kaunas to Warsaw. Its name refers to the organic gemstones — technically fossilized tree resin — that are harvested from the Baltic, and its course unites the three Baltic states, as well as linking them to the rest of the EU. The river Danube was once on the Roman frontier; it later became the high street of the Habsburgs. In the imperial color that recalls these two realms, the Purple Banana links Vienna to Bratislava, Budapest, and Belgrade. The Brenner Axis — stretching from Munich, Germany, via Innsbruck, Austria, to Bolzano and Verona in Italy — could be the Pink Banana . One tiny objection: This connection is regrettably straight. Perhaps the Brussels bureaucrats could make an exception to their famous rule about the bendiness of bananas so that this one could join the club. The Yellow Banana, running from Paris across Berlin to Warsaw, is arguably more important politically than it is economically, at least at this time. Here is French President Emmanuel Macron in 2023, receiving the then-leaders of Germany (Chancellor Olaf Scholz, left) and Poland (President Andrzej Duda, center) at the Élysée, the presidential palace in Paris. Credit : Andrea Savorani Neri/NurPhoto via Getty Images Squint, and you see Lotharingia Interestingly, many of these “new” corridors reconstitute economic zones and trade routes that are much older than the nation-states that sit on top of them. Squint, and the Blue Banana transforms into Lotharingia, the middle kingdom Lothair I received when Charlemagne’s empire was divided among his three grandsons at Verdun in 843. The Golden Banana follows the Via Domitia
